title: Four-sided stitch
subtitle: A pulled-thread border stitch that draws the fabric into a grid of open squares
excerpt: Four-sided stitch is a pulled-thread stitch worked on evenweave fabric with firm tension. Each unit is a square formed by four straight stitches, and the pulling action draws the fabric threads apart to leave a small hole at each corner. Repeated in rows, it builds geometric borders, grids, and openwork fillings characteristic of whitework and drawn-thread embroidery.
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (1886), drawn thread and pulled work chapters. Caulfeild and Saward, Dictionary of Needlework (1882), four-sided stitch entry.

content.text: Four-sided stitch is a counted, pulled-thread technique. It is worked on evenweave linen or cotton with a blunt tapestry needle and a firm, deliberate pull on every stitch. The thread itself is barely visible; the effect comes from the holes it opens in the fabric. A single unit covers a counted square of threads on the front of the fabric, but the needle travels diagonally on the back to reach the next corner, which is what creates the pulling force. Rows of units placed side by side form borders or all-over grid fillings.

items.label: Thread
items.value: Fine cotton thread, coton a broder no. 16 or 25, or a single strand of stranded cotton in a colour matching the fabric so the holes read clearly

items.label: Fabric
items.value: Evenweave linen, 28 to 32 count; the thread must be countable. Work over 4 fabric threads per side of each square

items.label: Needle
items.value: Tapestry needle size 24 or 26 (blunt tip essential to avoid splitting fabric threads)

items.label: Hoop
items.value: 18 to 20 cm hoop or a slate frame; fabric must be drum-taut for the pull to form clean holes

content.text: Secure the thread on the back. Bring the needle up at the bottom-left corner of the first square, point (A). Count 4 fabric threads to the right and take the needle down at point (B), the bottom-right corner. Pull firmly so the thread tightens against the weave. This is the bottom bar of the square.

On the back, slide the needle diagonally upward and bring it up at point (C), the top-right corner (4 threads above B). Take the needle back down at point (D), the top-left corner (4 threads to the left of C). Pull firmly. This is the top bar.

On the back, slide diagonally to bring the needle up again at (A). Take the needle up to (D), pulling firmly. This is the left bar. Then on the back, slide diagonally to (B) and take the needle up to (C), pulling firmly. This is the right bar. One complete square is now worked.

To continue the row, the needle is already at the top-right corner of the completed square. That corner becomes the top-left corner of the next square. Bring the needle out there and work the next unit in the same way. The shared bar between adjacent squares is worked only once.

Pull every stitch with the same steady force throughout. Inconsistent tension is the main cause of uneven holes. The holes form at the corners of each square where the diagonal back-stitches converge and draw the weave threads apart.

items.cause: The fabric is too loosely mounted, or the thread tension is too light.
items.fix: Re-mount the fabric drum-taut and use a deliberate, firm pull on each stitch. Match thread weight to fabric count: a thread heavier than the fabric thread will clog the hole rather than open it.

items.symptom: Squares are uneven or different sizes
items.cause: The thread count per side was not consistent, or the needle slipped fabric threads.
items.fix: Count carefully on every stitch. A blunt tapestry needle slips between threads cleanly; a sharp needle can pierce and distort the count.

items.symptom: Thread shows prominently rather than receding
items.cause: A thread too thick or too contrasting was used.
items.fix: Use a fine thread in a shade close to the fabric colour. Pulled-thread work is about the holes, not the thread.
